I don't find the distinction between social and biological to be useful as all diseases have a biological component.

In the case of depression, its prevalence today is caused by maladaptation of humans to the current environment. That is, depression is a response to the environment and had survival value for our ancestors, just like sickle cell anemia had survival advantage where malaria was prevalent. Today we have malaria under control, so sickle cell anemia becomes a debilitating disease.

The survival value of depression is conservation of energy and resources when the organism feels like things aren't going its way. Today food is plentiful and our survival doesn't depend on conservation of energy, so depression is maladaptive.

That is way oversimplifying things. Depression is a complex disease and isn't just about "conservation of energy". I doubt significant impairments in 5 out of the 9 of sleep, interest, guilt, energy, concentration, appetite, psychomotor retardation, and suicidality for two weeks ever held a survival advantage for an individual. Looking at things from an evo psych perspective, meaning there had to be some aggregate survival advantage, maybe depression stems as a maladaptive effect in the individual from some other thing that was adaptive in the population. A good circuit gone haywire perchance. That said, we can't ignore the loads of biology showing real deficits in neurotransmitters, real under activation globally of the brain, etc.

As an aside, I quoted social causation in my earlier post as that's the term the authors used in the Reddit post. I think the distinction between biology and social causation isn't super valuable in their context, especially since we know biology can effect social aspects, and social aspects can change the bio via epigenetics.
